name: Preppy / Ivy style

lead: Preppy, or Ivy, style gives a neat, classic collegiate look built on structured, traditional pieces. It grew from the dress of Northeastern US prep schools and Ivy League campuses, began in the early 1900s and was widespread by the late 1950s.

Typical staples include navy blazers, Oxford cloth button-down shirts, repp stripe ties, chinos, penny loafers, polo shirts and boat shoes. The style carries class and old-money associations. No published studies have tested whether it changes how attractive a person is judged to be.

paras: Wearers choose structured, traditional garments in a coordinated, conservative palette, combining pieces like an Oxford shirt, chinos and loafers. Fit is the main thing, and the pieces mix and match easily.
No health risks are documented. Cost depends on brand choices.

angle.text: Oxford shirts, chinos and loafers give you a neat, classic collegiate look that is visible the moment you put it on. It is a style tradition rather than something tested for attractiveness.

lead: Preppy, or Ivy, style is a way of dressing built around Oxford button-down shirts, chinos, navy blazers, penny loafers and polo shirts. People adopt it to look neat, put-together and quietly well-off, using fit and classic pieces rather than trends [1]. In looksmaxxing and style discussions it is a ready-made template: a small wardrobe of proven items that reads as clean and polished.

The style is associated with graduates of Northeastern US college-preparatory schools and with upper-class and old-money backgrounds [1]. Its menswear root, Ivy style, evolved on elite US campuses and was widespread by the late 1950s; Wikipedia's article on Ivy style cites a figure that about 70 percent of suits sold in 1957 and 1958 were in the Ivy style [1][2]. Core garments include the natural-shoulder sack jacket, button-down oxford shirts, unpleated trousers or khaki chinos, and penny loafers or brogues [2].

Interest has returned in waves: preppy emerged in the early 1980s as a return to Ivy styles, with Lisa Birnbach's 1980 The Official Preppy Handbook and brands such as Ralph Lauren; and in the early to mid 2020s the look came back as the "old money aesthetic" [1][2]. No published studies have tested whether preppy or Ivy dress changes how attractive a person is judged to be.

paras: The look draws on sailing, rowing and golf clothing and on British country wear such as tweed jackets and brogues.[1] Over time it became more relaxed, adding rugby shirts and boat shoes, with outfitters such as L.L. Bean, Eddie Bauer and Orvis supplying casual items.[1]
Fabrics and patterns commonly named include seersucker, madras and Nantucket red.[1]

J. Press and Brooks Brothers were key early retailers of Ivy style.[1] Women's preppy-influenced fashion emerged in the 1960s through Seven Sisters college students and designers such as Lilly Pulitzer and Perry Ellis.[1]

Lisa Birnbach's 1980 book The Official Preppy Handbook, a tongue-in-cheek guide to elite campus life, is credited with a 1980s revival, and Ralph Lauren, Lacoste and Izod brought the look to the mass market.[1] Interest declined in the 1990s, though brands such as J. Crew, Tommy Hilfiger and Vineyard Vines remain associated with it.[1]

Wikipedia's Ivy style article says the look evolved in the 1920s to 1940s by casualising formal menswear with British and American upper-class sportswear, and that veterans on the GI Bill wore khaki chinos to college in the late 1940s [2]. It was displaced in the late 1960s and early 1970s by the wide lapels and bright colours of the peacock revolution [2].

Take Ivy is a 1965 photography book by Teruyoshi Hayashida, Shosuke Ishizu, Kurosu Toshiyuki and Hajime Hasegawa, collecting candid photographs taken on Ivy League campuses between 1959 and 1965 [3]. It has sold more than 50,000 copies, was reissued by powerHouse Books in 2010, and is credited with influencing a mid-2010s neo-Ivy revival; Ralph Lauren and J. Crew have displayed copies in stores [3]. British Mods borrowed the look in the mid-1960s, according to Wikipedia's Ivy style article [2].
